(فَأَلْقى عَصاهُ فَإِذا هِيَ ثُعْبانٌ مُبِينٌ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; ألقى is a past verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; عصاه is the direct object. In فإذا the fāʾ is a conjunction and إذا is the "suddenness" إذا, which is an adverbial or a particle, and its discussion has already been given in detail; هي is the mubtadaʾ, ثعبان the khabar and مبين an adjective. The "wasp question" and the dispute of Sībawayh with al-Kisāʾī over it in the presence of Yaḥyā al-Barmakī has already been discussed. (وَنَزَعَ يَدَهُ فَإِذا هِيَ بَيْضاءُ لِلنَّاظِرِينَ) This sentence is conjoined to the one before it, and is like it in its parsing.
(قالَ لِلْمَلَإِ حَوْلَهُ إِنَّ هذا لَساحِرٌ عَلِيمٌ) قال فرعون; للملأ is attached to قال; حوله is an adverbial attached to an omitted element, a ḥāl. Al-Zamakhsharī has an ingenious treatment of its parsing, which we cite for its splendour:
"If you say: What governs حوله? I say: It is accusative in two ways, an accusative in form and an accusative in position. The governor of the formal accusative is what is implied in the adverbial, and the governor of the positional accusative is the accusative as ḥāl."
إن is a particle resembling the verb, and هذا is its noun; the lām is the shifted lām; ساحر is the khabar and عليم a second khabar. (يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُخْرِجَكُمْ مِنْ أَرْضِكُمْ بِسِحْرِهِ) The clause is an adjective of ساحر. It is a complete line of the majzūʾ al-rajaz metre, yet is not poetry, because intention is absent, and this has been discussed in detail before. أن and what is within its scope is the object of يريد; من أرضكم is attached to يخرجكم, and بسحره is also attached to يخرجكم.
(فَماذا تَأْمُرُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; ماذا is an interrogative noun, the direct object of تأمرون, or an absolute object because it is in the sense of a maṣdar; or ما is an interrogative noun and ذا a relative noun, the khabar, and the clause تأمرون the ṣila. He said that after what he had seen dazzled him and bewilderment and amazement overcame him. (قالُوا أَرْجِهْ وَأَخاهُ وَابْعَثْ فِي الْمَدائِنِ حاشِرِينَ) قالوا is a verb and agent; أرجه is an imperative verb and the hāʾ is the direct object; أخاه is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment) or is conjoined to the hāʾ; وابعث is conjoined to أرجه; في المدائن is attached to ابعث; and حاشرين is an adjective of an omitted direct object, that is, "police (shuraṭ) who will gather the magicians and bring them together". (يَأْتُوكَ بِكُلِّ سَحَّارٍ عَلِيمٍ) يأتوك is an imperfect verb, jussive because it is the answer to the imperative; بكل سحار is attached to يأتوك; and عليم is an adjective of سحار.

* Benefits:
Al-shurṭ: its singular is shurṭī. They are a group of the best of the helpers of rulers, and in our days they are the chiefs of the police and its men. They were so named because they made for themselves a mark by which they were known. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "Al-sharaṭ, with vowels on the letters, are the guards; they were so named because they made for themselves a mark by which they were known." Al-shurṭa is also the first battalion to take part in battle and to prepare for death.

dervis-irab:38-44.t:
* I'rab:
(فَجُمِعَ السَّحَرَةُ لِمِيقاتِ يَوْمٍ مَعْلُومٍ) The fāʾ is a conjunction upon an implied element; جمع is a passive past verb and السحرة the deputy agent; لميقات is a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to جمع; يوم is a muḍāf ilayhi and معلوم an adjective. The "known day" is the day of adornment (yawm al-zīna), and its appointed time is the forenoon (waqt al-ḍuḥā); its mention has already passed in [Sūrat] Ṭāhā, so he renewed the reference with it. (وَقِيلَ لِلنَّاسِ: هَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُجْتَمِعُونَ؟) وقيل is conjoined to what precedes; للناس is attached to it; هل is a particle of interrogation; أنتم is a mubtadaʾ and مجتمعون its khabar; the clause is the content of the saying. In the interrogation there is the sense of a command, as though he were finding them slow and urging them to gather. Among this is the saying of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:
هل أنت باعث دينار لحاجتنا ... أو عبد رب أخا عوف بن مخراق
(Gloss: Will you send Dīnār for our need, or ʿAbd Rabb, the brother of ʿAwf ibn Mikhrāq?)
Here هل is an interrogative of impatience (istifhām istibṭāʾī) containing an urging to act. دينار is the name of a man, and رب likewise, and it is accusative because it is conjoined to the position of دينار, since it is an object in meaning; أخا عوف is an adjective of it, and it is said to be a vocative. ʿAwf and Mikhrāq are the names of two men, and it is reported "ʿAwn" with a nūn. (لَعَلَّنا نَتَّبِعُ السَّحَرَةَ إِنْ كانُوا هُمُ الْغالِبِينَ) The clause is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, because the hope is with regard to the state of victory which requires following, though their original intention was that they should not follow Moses; the meaning is: hoping that victory would be theirs so that Moses would not be followed. لعل with its noun, and the clause نتبع is its khabar; السحرة is the direct object; إن is conditional; كانوا is the protasis, being kāna with its noun; هم is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) and الغالبين the khabar of كانوا. (فَلَمَّا جاءَ السَّحَرَةُ قالُوا لِفِرْعَوْنَ أَإِنَّ لَنا لَأَجْراً إِنْ كُنَّا نَحْنُ الْغالِبِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; لما is temporal, adverbial, or a connective; جاء السحرة is a verb and agent; the clause قالوا has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive condition; لفرعون is attached to قالوا; the hamza is interrogative; إن is a particle resembling the verb; لنا is its fronted khabar and أجرا its postponed noun; إن is conditional; كنا is kāna with its noun and is the protasis; نحن is a separating pronoun and الغالبين the khabar of كنا; and the apodosis of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes, because his words أئن لنا لأجرا are in the sense of the apodosis, as they indicate it. (قالَ نَعَمْ وَإِنَّكُمْ إِذاً لَمِنَ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ) قال فرعون; نعم is a particle of answer, that is, "you shall have the reward"; and he added to them with his words وإنكم, which is a conjunction; إن with its noun; إذن is a particle of answer and requital; the lām is the shifted lām; and من المقربين is the khabar of إن. He promised them the reward and nearness and standing with him. (قالَ لَهُمْ مُوسى أَلْقُوا ما أَنْتُمْ مُلْقُونَ) قال لهم موسى is a verb and agent; لهم is attached to قال; the clause ألقوا is the content of the saying; ما is the direct object; the clause أنتم ملقون is the ṣila; أنتم is a mubtadaʾ and ملقون its khabar. (فَأَلْقَوْا حِبالَهُمْ وَعِصِيَّهُمْ وَقالُوا بِعِزَّةِ فِرْعَوْنَ إِنَّا لَنَحْنُ الْغالِبُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; ألقوا is a verb and agent; حبالهم is the direct object; عصيهم is conjoined to حبالهم; وقالوا is conjoined to فألقوا. In بعزة the bāʾ is a particle of oath and of genitive, and عزة is genitive by the bāʾ; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "we swear and take oath by the might of Pharaoh". إنا is إن with its noun, its hamza being obligatorily kasra because it follows an oath, as has gone before; the lām is the shifted lām; نحن is a separating pronoun or a mubtadaʾ; and الغالبون is the khabar of إنا or the khabar of نحن, the clause being the khabar of إنا.

dervis-irab:45-51.t:
* I'rab:
(فَأَلْقى مُوسى عَصاهُ فَإِذا هِيَ تَلْقَفُ ما يَأْفِكُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; ألقى موسى عصاه is a verb, agent and direct object; in فإذا the fāʾ is a conjunction and إذا is the "suddenness" إذا; هي is a mubtadaʾ and the clause تلقف its khabar; ما is the direct object and the clause يأفكون is the ṣila of ما, that is, "it swallows what they turn away from its true face by their deceptive embellishment, and forge". (فَأُلْقِيَ السَّحَرَةُ ساجِدِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; ألقي is a passive past verb and السحرة the deputy agent. The agent for whom the direct object stood in, had it been stated, is Allah the Mighty and Majestic, through the success He inspired in them, or their faith, or what they witnessed of the dazzling miracle before which the matter of magic shrank. More discussion of "casting" (ilqāʾ) will come in the chapter on rhetoric. ساجدين is a ḥāl [Translator's note: the source prints «ماجدين», evidently a misprint for «ساجدين»]. (قالُوا آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ) The clause آمنا, of verb and agent, is the content of the saying; برب العالمين is attached to آمنا; and the clause of saying is a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) from ألقي, or a ḥāl with an implied قد. (رَبِّ مُوسى وَهارُونَ) رب is a badal from رب العالمين, or an ʿaṭf bayān; موسى وهارون is a muḍāf ilayhi. (قالَ آمَنْتُمْ لَهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ آذَنَ لَكُمْ) The clause آمنتم is the content of the saying; له is attached to آمنتم, and the adverbial likewise; أن and what is within its scope is in the position of genitive by annexation; and لكم is attached to آذن.
(إِنَّهُ لَكَبِيرُكُمُ الَّذِي عَلَّمَكُمُ السِّحْرَ فَلَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ) A justification of their submission to Moses and Aaron, and a deception of his people, lest they believe that the magicians had believed with insight and the appearance of truth. إن with its noun; the shifted lām; كبيركم is the khabar of إن; الذي is an adjective; the clause علمكم is the ṣila; the kāf is a first direct object and السحر a second direct object. In فلسوف the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ, that is, "if you persist in what you did, then you will soon know the evil consequence of what you did"; the lām is the preparatory lām of an oath; سوف is a particle of the future; and تعلمون is an imperfect verb and agent, the object being omitted as we have implied.
(لَأُقَطِّعَنَّ أَيْدِيَكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ مِنْ خِلافٍ وَلَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ) The lām is the preparatory lām of an oath; لأقطعن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on the fatḥa because of its attachment to the heavy nūn of emphasis, and the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I"; the clause has no grammatical position because it is explicative, serving as clarification of what he left vague with his words فلسوف تعلمون; أيديكم is the direct object; أرجلكم is conjoined to أيديكم; and من خلاف is a ḥāl, that is, joined together: each one's right hand with his left foot. This has been discussed before. ولأصلبنكم is conjoined to لأقطعن, and أجمعين is an emphasis (tawkīd) of the kāf. (قالُوا: لا ضَيْرَ إِنَّا إِلى رَبِّنا مُنْقَلِبُونَ) لا is the lā of generic negation and its noun is indeclinable on the fatḥa, and its khabar is omitted, that is, "there is no harm upon us and no distress" [Translator's note: the source prints «لا ضمير علينا», evidently a misprint for «لا ضير علينا»; here and in the preceding clause it reads «ضمير اسمها», "its noun, a pronoun"; translated as written]. The clause إنا is a justification for the absence of harm; إن with its noun; إلى ربنا is attached to منقلبون; and منقلبون is the khabar of إنا. (إِنَّا نَطْمَعُ أَنْ يَغْفِرَ لَنا رَبُّنا خَطايانا أَنْ كُنَّا أَوَّلَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ) إن with its noun, and the clause نطمع its khabar, the agent being latent, its implied form being "we". أن and what is within its scope is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "in the forgiveness of our sins"; or else by incorporating into نطمع the sense of نرجو ("we hope"), so that أن and what is within its scope is in the position of accusative as an object. ربنا is the agent of يغفر and خطايانا the direct object. أن and what is within its scope is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "because we were", or the bāʾ, so that the implication is "by reason of our being"; كان with its noun, and أول المؤمنين its khabar, that is, the first of those who believed among Pharaoh's subjects.

* Rhetoric:
In his words «فألقي السحرة ساجدين» there is a metaphor with the vehicle omitted (istiʿāra makniyya), as though they were seized and flung upon their faces. What has added beauty to this metaphor is conformity (mushākala), because he expressed the falling prostrate by "were cast" (ulqiya) and did not say "so they fell down prostrate", in conformity with the earlier castings.

dervis-irab:176-191.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْأَيْكَةِ): In the language, a dense tree; its plural is أيك. The Qāmūs says: "أيك يأيك (of the pattern تعب) أيكا, and استأيك الشجر: the trees became intertwined and formed an أيكة. The أيك is the dense, intertwined trees, the singular being أيكة." So الأيكة is applied to a single one of the أيك, and to a thicket of intertwined trees near Madyan. They said: their tree was the dūm (doum palm), and it was the village of Shuʿayb, named after its builder Madyan ibn Ibrāhīm, eight days' journey from Egypt. The Qur'an commentators and the lexicographers disagreed about it, and we shall quote some of what they said.
Al-Zamakhsharī said:
"أصحاب الأيكة was read with the hamza and without it (with the hamza dropped), and in the genitive as an annexation, which is the sound reading. As for whoever read it in the accusative and claimed that ليكة, on the pattern of ليلة, is the name of a town, that is a delusion to which the script of the muṣḥaf led him, since it is written in this sūra and in Sūrat (Ṣād) without an alif. There are things in the muṣḥaf written contrary to the analogy of the conventional orthography; it was written thus in these two sūras only according to the pronunciation of the speaker, just as the grammarians write لان and لولا in this form to show the pronunciation of the lightened form; and in the rest of the Qur'an it is written in the original way, and the story is one. Besides, ليكة is a name that is not known. It is reported that the أصحاب الأيكة were people of intertwined trees, and their tree was the dūm."
Al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī said:
"In one reading, with the hamza dropped, its vowel cast onto the lām, and with fatḥa on the hāʾ (sic: the final letter); it is a thicket of trees near Madyan." This procedure implies that the existing lām is the lām of definiteness, and in that case his statement "and with fatḥa on the hāʾ" is not sound, since a noun joined with al, whether definite or otherwise, is put in the genitive with kasra, whether a transfer (of the vowel) has occurred in it or not. Some explained the fatḥa by saying that the noun is on the pattern of ليلة, so the lām is part of the structure of the word and there is no transfer, but rather the vowel of the lām is original; so putting it in the genitive with fatḥa is then clear.
Al-Shihāb al-Khafājī said:
"Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and others found this reading problematic, because there is no ground for the fatḥa, since the transfer of the vowel of the hamza does not require changing the case ending from kasra to fatḥa. The answer given is that ليكة in this reading is the name of the town, and it is not fully declined (ghayr muṣrafa) because of being a proper name and feminine; and the lām in it is part of the word, not the definite article, because that would require full declension. So the claim of the one who says it rests on a transfer is incorrect. With this, what the grammarians said is refuted, for they ascribed this reading to corruption."
Al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī went on at great length in justifying this reading, and his text is:
Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir read ليكة with a single lām and with fatḥa on the tāʾ (sic), making it a noun not defined by al, with أصحاب annexed to it, here and in (Ṣād) in particular; and the others read الأيكة, defined by al, in agreement with what is unanimously agreed in (al-Ḥijr) and in (Qāf). People's statements about the first reading are confused, and some of them were bold against its reciter, and I shall mention a portion of that for you. Its justification, according to what Abū ʿUbayda said, is that ليكة is the name of the village in which they lived, while الأيكة is the name of the whole country, so the difference between them is like the difference between Makka and Bakka.
The author of the Qāmūs said:
"Whoever reads الأيكة, it is the thicket; whoever reads ليكة, it is the name of the village, and its place is (under the letter) lām. In al-Bukhārī the form اللائكة, plural of أيكة, occurs, and it seems to be an error."
His commentator in al-Tāj said:
"His saying 'and it seems to be an error' is because it has no ground and none of the imams spoke it; but he (may Allah be pleased with him) is trustworthy in what he transmits, so one should think well of him, and his commentators answered for him and declared it sound."
Abū al-Baqāʾ said:
"أصحاب الأيكة is read with kasra on the tāʾ, with the hamza pronounced fully, or lightened by casting (its vowel), like الأنثى and الأنثى. ليكة has been read with a yāʾ after the lām and fatḥa on the tāʾ, but this does not hold, since ليكة does not exist in the language so as to be made a proper name; and if it is claimed that the hamza was turned into a lām, that is extremely far-fetched."
The أيك and the doves in poetry:
The أيك and its doves have captivated the poets, and their poems about it are many. Abū Ḥātim recited, from a man of Banū Nahshal:
ألام على فيض الدموع وإنني ... بفيض الدموع الجاريات جدير
أيبكي حمام الأيك من فقد إلفه ... وأصبر عنها إنني لصبور
(I am blamed for the overflowing of my tears, though I deserve the flowing tears. Shall the dove of the thicket weep for the loss of its mate, while I endure the loss of her? I am indeed patient.)
Al-Riyāshī recited from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Muntajiʿ ibn Nabhān recited to me, from a man of Banū al-Ṣayyidāʾ:
دعت فوق أفنان من الأيك موهنا ... مطوقة ورقاء في إثر آلف
فهاجت عقابيل الهوى إذ ترنمت ... وشبت ضرام الشوق تحت الشراسف
بكت بجفون دمعها غير ذارف ... وأغرت جفوني بالدموع الذّوارف
(Late at night, above the branches of the thicket, a collared, ash-grey dove called out after a mate. When she trilled, she stirred the remnants of passion and kindled the blaze of longing beneath the ribs. She wept with eyelids whose tears did not fall, and she incited my eyelids to shed pouring tears.)
The curious thing in this chapter is the saying of ʿAwf ibn Muḥallim:
ألا يا حمام الأيك إلفك حاضر ... وغصنك ميّاد ففيم تنوح
أفق لا تنح من غير شيء فإنني ... بكيت زمانا والفؤاد صحيح
ولوعا فشطّت غربه دار زينب ... فها أنا أبكي والفؤاد جريح
(O dove of the thicket, your mate is present and your branch sways; so why do you mourn? Wake up, do not mourn for nothing, for I wept for a time while my heart was sound, in ardent love; then the abode of Zaynab grew distant, so now I weep while my heart is wounded.) [Translator's note: the third verse is garbled in the source (غربه, "its edge", seems out of place); translated as best it can be understood.]
(القسطاس): With kasra or ḍamma on the qāf, and it has been read with both: the straight balance. If it derives from القسط, which is justice, and the ʿayn (i.e. the sīn) is regarded as repeated, then its pattern is فعلاس; otherwise it is quadriliteral. It is also said that it means "justice" in Greek (Rūmī).
(وَلا تَعْثَوْا): And do not spread corruption. One says عثا في الأرض and عثي, and that is like highway robbery, raiding and destroying crops. In al-Mukhtār: "عثا في الأرض: he corrupted; its pattern is that of سما; and عثي with kasra, عثوا also, and عثى with two fatḥas on the pattern of فتى. Allah the Exalted said: 'ولا تعثوا في الأرض مفسدين'." I say: al-Azharī said: "The readers all agree on fatḥa of the thāʾ, which indicates that the Qur'an was revealed in the second dialect."
(وَالْجِبِلَّةَ): With kasra on the jīm and the bāʾ and with shadda on the vowelled lām: the unified, coarse creation. In the Qāmūs: "الجبلة, الجبلة, الجبلة and الجبلّة—and this last is the one read—: the face and what faces you of it, the build, the nature, the origin, strength, and hardness of the ground." الجبل with fatḥa on the jīm and sukūn on the bāʾ is the verbal noun of جبله الله على كذا, i.e. He moulded and created him thus; and the name of the nature is جبلة. This word, in this sense, has many synonyms: الجبلة, الخيم, الطبع, النحيزة, الطبيعة, النبيتة, الضريبة, السجية, الشنشنة, الخليقة, السليقة, السليقة (sic), الشيمة, الغريزة, النجار. Some have versified the meanings of الجبل, saying:
قد جبل الله الطباع جبلا ... وسمي المال الكثير جبلا
وعدد الناس الكثير جبلا ... بالضم إن أردت أو بالكسر
وجه وقوة وغيث جبلة ... وامرأة غليظة والجبلة
جماعة أو كثرة كالجبله ... لقدح من خشب ذي كبر
(Allah has moulded natures, jabalan; abundant wealth is also called jabal; and a great number of people is jabal, with ḍamma if you wish, or with kasra; a face, strength and rain, jibla; a coarse woman, and the jibla; a group or a multitude like the jabla; for a large wooden cup.) [Translator's note: the verses are obscure and appear corrupt in the source; the gloss is approximate.]
(كِسَفاً): With kasra on the kāf and fatḥa on the sīn; it has also been read كسفا with sukūn on the sīn, and both are plurals of كسفة, like قطع and سدر. Abū ʿUbayda said: "الكسف is the plural of كسفة, like سدر and سدرة; al-Sulamī and Ḥafṣ read كسفا, also the plural of كسفة, which is the piece and the side, like كسرة and كسر." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "الكسفة is a piece of a thing; one says 'give me a كسفة of your garment', i.e. a piece; and one says الكسف and الكسفة are the same." Al-Akhfash said: "Whoever read كسفا from the sky made it singular, and whoever read كسفا made it a plural."
(الظُّلَّةِ): The narrow shade, and what one takes shade under from heat or cold, and whatever shades you, such as a tree; the plural is ظلل and ظلال. The "Day of the Ẓulla" became famous through their punishment: a cloud hovered above them and shaded them after intense heat had struck them, and it rained fire upon them, so they were burned up.

* I'rab:
(كَذَّبَ أَصْحابُ الْأَيْكَةِ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) A resumptive statement, uttered to mention the seventh and last story in this sūra. (إِذْ قالَ لَهُمْ شُعَيْبٌ أَلا تَتَّقُونَ) This verse and those after it have been covered in all seven stories, and the secret of that will come in the chapter on rhetoric. He did not say "their brother" as He said of the prophets before him, because he was not of the أصحاب الأيكة by lineage; when He mentioned Madyan, He said "their brother Shuʿayb" because he was of them. (إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ، فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ، وَما أَسْئَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْرٍ إِنْ أَجْرِيَ إِلَّا عَلى رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ) Verses covered in the seven stories. (أَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ وَلا تَكُونُوا مِنَ الْمُخْسِرِينَ) أوفوا is an imperative verb and fāʿil (agent), الكيل is mafʿūl bihi (direct object), the wāw is a conjunction, لا is prohibitive, تكونوا is an imperfect defective verb jussive by لا, the wāw is its ism (subject), and من المخسرين is the khabar (predicate) of تكونوا. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Measuring is of three kinds: full, scanty, and excessive. He commanded the obligatory, which is giving full measure, and forbade the forbidden, which is giving scanty measure, and did not mention the excessive; it seems that leaving it out of both command and prohibition is evidence that if one does it, he has done well, and if he does not, there is no blame on him." (وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ) Its i'rab is clear. (وَلا تَبْخَسُوا النَّاسَ أَشْياءَهُمْ وَلا تَعْثَوْا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction, لا is prohibitive, تبخسوا is an imperfect verb jussive by لا, the wāw is fāʿil, الناس is the first mafʿūl bihi and أشياعهم is the second mafʿūl bihi. [Translator's note: the source writes أشياعهم; the Qur'anic word is أَشْياءَهُمْ.]
Among their sayings: "لا تبخس أخاك حقه" (Do not diminish your brother of his right). And ولا تعثوا is conjoined to ولا تبخسوا, في الأرض is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to تعثوا, and مفسدين is a ḥāl (circumstantial) confirming the meaning of its governing verb, although the two words differ in form. (وَاتَّقُوا الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالْجِبِلَّةَ الْأَوَّلِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction, اتقوا is an imperative verb and fāʿil, الذي is mafʿūl bihi, the clause خلقكم is the ṣila, الجبلة is conjoined to الذي, and الأولين is an adjective of الجبلة. (قالُوا إِنَّما أَنْتَ مِنَ الْمُسَحَّرِينَ) إنما is kāffa and makfūfa (a restricting particle and the restricted), أنت is mubtadaʾ and من المسحرين is khabar; the sentence is the content of the speech (maqūl al-qawl). (وَما أَنْتَ إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُنا وَإِنْ نَظُنُّكَ لَمِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction, ما is negative, أنت is mubtadaʾ, إلا is a particle of restriction, بشر is khabar, and مثلنا is an adjective of بشر; the wāw is a conjunction, إن is the lightened form of the heavy (إنّ) and its ism is omitted, نظنك is an imperfect verb in the nominative, its fāʿil a latent pronoun, its implied form being "نحن", and the kāf is mafʿūl bihi; the lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa), and من الكاذبين is a khabar. Al-Zamakhsharī said:
"If you say: the lightened إنّ and its lām—how did they come to be separated by the verb ظن and the second of its two objects? I say: the original is that they are separated by the mubtadaʾ and khabar, as in إن زيد لمنطلق. Since the two chapters—I mean the chapter of كان and the chapter of ظننت—are of the same kind as the chapter of mubtadaʾ and khabar, it was done in both chapters, so it was said إن كان زيد لمنطلقا and إن ظننته لمنطلقا." (فَأَسْقِطْ عَلَيْنا كِسَفاً مِنَ السَّماءِ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ) The fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (eloquent fāʾ), أسقط is an imperative verb, علينا is attached to أسقط, كسفا is mafʿūl bihi, and من السماء is an adjective of كسفا; إن is conditional, كنت is a past defective verb in the position of jussive, the protasis, the tāʾ is its ism, and من الصادقين is the khabar of كنت; the apodosis is omitted, indicated by what precedes, i.e. "فأسقط علينا". (قالَ رَبِّي أَعْلَمُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ) ربي is mubtadaʾ and أعلم is khabar; the sentence is the content of the speech; بما is attached to أعلم, and the clause تعملون has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of the relative. (فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَخَذَهُمْ عَذابُ يَوْمِ الظُّلَّةِ إِنَّهُ كانَ عَذابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, كذبوه is a verb, fāʿil and mafʿūl bihi; فأخذهم is a verb and mafʿūl bihi, and عذاب يوم الظلة is fāʿil; إنّ and its ism, and the clause كان is its khabar; the ism of كان is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "هو", عذاب is the khabar of كان, يوم is muḍāf ilayhi, and عظيم is an adjective. (إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً وَما كانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ، وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ) Its i'rab has been covered.

* Rhetoric:
The art of repetition (al-takrīr):
In these seven stories He repeated at the beginning of each story and at its end what He repeated, to which we have pointed, because repetition fixes meanings in the souls and roots them in the breasts, while attaching each one to a reason. The art of repetition is subtle in its approach, and it is often confused by most people sometimes with iṭnāb (expansiveness) and sometimes with taṭwīl (prolixity). It is divided into two kinds:
The first kind of repetition:
It is found in both the wording and the meaning, as when you say to someone you are summoning: "Hurry, hurry", and of it is the saying of Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī:
ولم أر مثل جيراني ومثلي ... لمثلي عند مثلهم مقام
(I have not seen the like of my neighbours, nor the like of me, for one like me to stay with the like of them.)
The second kind of repetition:
It is found in the meaning without the wording, as when you say: "Obey me and do not disobey my commands", for the command to obey is a prohibition of disobedience.
In any case, there is nothing repeated in the Qur'an whose repetition has no benefit.
Some people claimed that Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī brought a repetition that he had no need for in his saying:
العارض الهتن بن العارض الهتن بن العا ... رض الهتن بن العارض الهتن
(The pouring cloud, son of the pouring cloud, son of the pouring cloud, son of the pouring cloud.)
But there is no repetition in this verse; it is like saying "the one described by such-and-such, son of the one described by such-and-such", i.e. he is deeply rooted in lineage in this description. Something similar occurs in the Prophetic ḥadīth, as in his saying ﷺ describing the Prophet Yūsuf: "The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yūsuf ibn Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm." So the verse is like the Prophetic ḥadīth in meaning, but falls below the ḥadīth in its wording; these are words that are fine when used singly, but bringing them in this interlocking manner is what disfigured their beauty and turned them into a kind of verbal sophistry that diminished them. This matter is referred to taste alone, which is the arbiter that judges in such matters. How well the French philosopher Voltaire said: "Your taste is your teacher."
Unprofitable repetition:
If the repetition is not beneficial, it is gross inarticulacy (ʿiyy). It is strange that a poet like Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī should fall into it and bring the verse we cited at the beginning of this discussion, namely:
ولم أر مثل جيراني ومثلي ... لمثلي عند مثلهم مقام
Do you not see that he says: "I have not seen the like of my neighbours in the badness of neighbourliness, nor the like of me in accompanying them and my staying with them"? Yet he repeated this meaning twice in the verse. Like it is his saying:
وقلقلت بالهم الذي قلقل الحشا ... قلاقل دهر كلهن قلاقل
(I shook with the care that shook the entrails, the upheavals of an age, all of them upheavals.)
And likewise his saying:
عظمت فلما لم تكلم مهابة ... تواضعت وهو العظم عظما على عظم
(You were great, and when out of awe none could speak to you, you humbled yourself, and that is greatness upon greatness.)
One of the ancient critics said of it: "Had this verse been called a graveyard, it would have suited it." It seems that this critic dislikes repetition, and his dislike pictured to him Ibn al-Rūmī's poem about the woman, which begins:
أجنت لك الوجد أغصان وكثبان ... فيهنّ نوعان تفّاح ورمان
(Branches and dunes have harvested passion for you; in them are two kinds, apples and pomegranates.)
as not beautiful, or of that sort, so he said: "This is the house of the watermelon; read its love-prelude and you will know it." [Translator's note: the sentence is somewhat garbled in the source; translated as written.]
We do not deny that Ibn al-Rūmī exaggerated in his love poetry for her and mentioned jujubes, ban-trees and narcissus at length, but it falls in its proper place and there is no way to attack it.
We return to Abū al-Ṭayyib, who repeated so much that he became low in many of his verses, though he is the foremost poet of Arabic. He said:
أسد فرائسها الأسود يقودها ... أسد تصير له الأسود ثعالبا
(A lion whose prey are lions, led by a lion before whom lions become foxes.)
Ibn Rashīq said: "I do not know how he escaped from this thicket full of lions." And al-Aṣmaʿī said to one who recited to him the saying:
فما للنوى جذ النوى قطع النوى ... كذاك النوى قطّاعة لوصال
(What ails separation, that it cut the date-stones, severed the stones? Thus separation is a cutter-off of union.)
"If Allah set a sheep upon this date-stone, it would eat it all."
As for the saying of Abū Nuwās:
أقمنا بها يوما ويوما وثالثا ... ويوما له يوم الترحل خامس
(We stayed there a day, and a day, and a third, and a day whose fifth is the day of departure.)
Ibn al-Athīr said in al-Mathal al-sāʾir: "His intention is that they stayed four days. How strange that he brings a verse as feeble as this, indicating gross inarticulacy, amid those wonderfully beautiful verses, which are:
ودار ندامى عطلوها وأدلجوا ... بها أثر منهم جديد ودارس
مساحب من جر الزقاق على الثرى ... وأضغاث ريحان جنيّ ويابس
حبست بها صحبي فجددت عهدهم ... وإني على أمثال تلك لحابس
تدار علينا الراح في عسجدية ... حبتها بأنواع التصاوير
فارس قرارتها كسرى وفي جنباتها ... مها تدريها بالقسيّ الف
وارس فللرّاح ما زرّت عليه جيوبها ... وللماء ما دارت عليه القلانس
(An abode of drinking companions who abandoned it and set out at night; in it are traces of them, fresh and effaced: trails where wineskins were dragged over the earth, and bundles of basil, fresh and dry. I held my companions there and renewed their covenant, and I am one who halts at the like of those. The wine is passed around among us in a golden cup that she endowed with varied pictures; Persian, its bottom is Chosroes, and in its sides are wild cows that horsemen chase with bows. To the wine belongs what their collars are buttoned over, and to the water what their caps encircle.)" [Translator's note: the last two verses are garbled in the source (the word division "الف / وارس" is broken across the hemistich); translated as best it can be understood.]
But Ibn al-Athīr erred and misunderstood the verse and did not examine it closely before criticising it; had he examined it closely he would not have said this. The correct meaning is that the stay was six days, because he said "and a third", and "a day" (another) whose fifth was the day on which we departed. [Translator's note: the source says "six days" (سبة أيام, sic, for ستة); this is translated as written.]
Abū Nuwās is too exalted in rank to be feeble and to bring this expression for no weighty meaning; in wine poetry he has verses without equal, which can be subtle to the understanding. It is related of him that his saying was mentioned before al-Rashīd:
فاسقني البكر التي اعتجرت ... بخمار الشيب في الرحم
(So give me to drink the virgin wine that wrapped itself in the veil of grey hair in the womb.)
Al-Rashīd said to those present: "What does it mean?" One of them said: "When wine is in its jar, something like foam is on it; that is the grey hair he meant." Al-Aṣmaʿī was present and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Abū ʿAlī is too exalted in rank and his meanings are hidden; ask him about it." He was brought and asked, and said: "When the vine first brings out the cluster on the vine-shoot, there is on it something that resembles cotton." Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "Did I not tell you that Abū Nuwās has a subtler eye than you said?"
Back to the verses:
We return and say: the Qur'an repeated these verses at the beginning and end of each story because these stories were drummed upon ears afflicted with deafness and hearts covered over, so there was no alternative to returning to them with reiteration and repetition, in the hope that this might open their locks and clear away the rust that had corroded them. And there will come, of repetition in the Qur'an, what intoxicates souls and captivates minds.

dervis-irab:123-140.t:
* Vocabulary:
(رِيعٍ): «Al-rīʿ», with kasra or fatḥa on the rāʾ. He said in al-Asās and al-Lisān:
"They alighted at a «rīʿ» and a «rayʿ rafīʿ» and a «rīʿa» and a «rayʿa rafīʿa», meaning raised ground. You say: «They build on every rīʿa, while their kingdom is like a mirage in a plain»." He said in al-Qāmūs: "«Al-rīʿ», with kasra and with fatḥa, is raised ground, or any mountain pass, or any road, or the road that opens out in a mountain, and the raised mountain; the singular is with tāʾ marbūṭa ... With kasra it is the hermitage, the dovecote and the high hill ... and with fatḥa it is the surplus of everything, like the «rīʿ» of dough, flour and seed." I say: its use in the sense of yield is correct. One says "food of much «rīʿ»"; «arāʿat al-ḥinṭa» and «rāʿat» mean the wheat prospered; Allah the Exalted made it prosper; and «arāʿa al-nās hādhā al-ʿām» means their crops prospered this year. They say "how much is the «rīʿ» of your land", meaning its yield. Al-Musayyab ibn ʿAlas said:
في الآل يرفعها ويخفضها ... ريع يلوح كأنه سحل
(In the mirage a rīʿ raises them and lowers them, gleaming as if it were a garment of fine cloth.)
The pronoun in the verse refers to the howdahs (women's litters): they are in the mirage, which is the «sarāb», and a «rīʿ», that is, a road, now raised and now lowered, or a high place, raises them as it ascends and lowers them as it descends. One says "he has no «rīʿ»", meaning no return and no yield.
(آيَةً): «Al-āya» is a landmark by which passers-by are guided. Building it was for sport and play, because they were guided by the stars on their journeys and had no need of it. It was also said that what is meant is lofty palaces, whose building you raise and in which you gather, and you make sport of those who pass by you.
(تَعْبَثُونَ): In al-Miṣbāḥ: "«ʿabitha ʿabthan», of the pattern «taʿiba», means he played and did what has no benefit; he is a «ʿābith»."
(مَصانِعَ): Plural of «maṣnaʿa», with fatḥa on the mīm and either fatḥa or ḍamma on the nūn. It is the basin or the pool, so His word «maṣāniʿ» means basins and pools in which you collect water; they are of the kind of cisterns. In al-Mukhtār: "«Al-maṣnaʿa», with fatḥa on the mīm and ḍamma or fatḥa on the nūn, is like a basin in which rain water is collected; and «al-maṣāniʿ» are the fortresses." In al-Qāmūs and its commentary al-Tāj: "«Al-maṣnaʿa» and «al-maṣnaʿa», with fatḥa on the mīm and fatḥa or ḍamma on the nūn, is that in which rain water is collected like a basin, and the plural is «maṣāniʿ». «Al-maṣāniʿ» also are:
the castles, the fortresses and the palaces. «Al-maṣnaʿa» is also an invitation to eat; one says 'we were at the «maṣnaʿa» of so-and-so'; and a place set apart for bees, far from houses." All of these meanings are suitable for the exegesis.
(بَطَشْتُمْ): «Al-baṭsh» is violence and seizing with force. The letters bāʾ with ṭāʾ as first and second radicals of a word have a particular, strange character: they indicate violence, strength and disregard for others. (Translator's note: what follows in the source is a long digressive list of words from the roots b-ṭ-ʾ, b-ṭ-ḥ, b-ṭ-kh, b-ṭ-r, b-ṭ-l and b-ṭ-n, many of which are not of the same root as «baṭsh»; it is translated as written.) One says: «abṭaʾa ʿalayya fulān», and «baṭuʾa fī mashyatihi», and «tabāṭaʾa fī amrihi», and «tabāṭaʾa ʿannī», and "in him is slowness" (buṭʾ), and "I was not slow", and "I have been slow", and a slow horse among slow horses, and "what made you late to us?", "what slowed you?", "what made you slow?" ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
فقمت أمشي فقامت وهي فاترة ... كشارب الرّاح بطّا مشيه السكر
(I rose and walked, and she rose languid, like a drinker of wine whose walk is slowed by drunkenness.)
It is not hidden how much of all this is self-importance, arrogance and disregard of others. One says «baṭaḥahu ʿalā wajhihi fa-inbaṭaḥa» (he threw him on his face and he fell prostrate), and in it is all humiliation, abasement and contempt. Ḥuwayṣ looked at the grave of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl and said, "He is the length of my prostration", meaning the length of his stature lying face down on the ground. «Biṭāḥ» are wide, broad level plains (baṭḥāʾ); «tabaṭṭaḥa al-sayl» means the torrent's course widened. Dhū al-Rumma said:
ولا زال من نوء السماك عليكما ... ونوء الثريا وابل متبطّح
(May there never cease upon you both, from the rain-star of al-Simāk and the rain-star of the Pleiades, a spreading downpour.)
«Tabaṭṭaḥa fulān» means he took up residence in the wide valley bed (al-abṭaḥ). He said:
هلّا سألت عن الذين تبطحوا ... كرم البطاح وخير سرّة وادي
(Why did you not ask about those who settled the noble plains, the best centre of a valley?)
«Abṭakha al-qawm» and «aqthaʾū» mean they had abundant melons and cucumbers. Al-Layth looked at a people eating melon and said:
لما رأيت المبطخين أبطخوا ... فأكلوا منه ومنه لطخوا
(When I saw the melon-folk had plenty of melons, they ate of it and smeared themselves with it.)
And "I saw him going round among the kitchens and the melon patches", and only a proud man boasting of his wealth and riches does that. «Baṭira fulān» means he exceeded the limit in arrogance and exuberance; a man «ashir baṭir»; wealth made him insolent (abṭarahu). Among their sayings: "It did not rain until it made insolent", meaning the sky, and that fertility makes people insolent, as he said:
قوم إذا اخضرّت نعالهم ... يتناهقون تناهق الحمر
(A people who, when their sandals turn green, bray as donkeys bray.)
A woman «baṭīra» is one of intense insolence. «Bayṭara al-dābba» means he treated the animal as a veterinarian (bayṭār); and "more famous than the banner of the veterinarian"; and "the world is a harlot, one day with a perfumer and one day with a veterinarian". Among their sayings also: "I remember him, he being a veterinarian to our animals; today he is a ruler over us." Among their transmitted maxims: "Do not make your companion insolent by his capacity (dharʿuhu)", that is, do not disturb his ability and do not provoke him by burdening him beyond what he can bear; «dharʿuhu» is a badal al-ishtimāl (inclusive substitute). «Baṭira fulān niʿmat Allāh» means he took it lightly and so was ungrateful for it, and did not weigh it so as to be thankful; of this is «baṭirat maʿīshatahā» (it was insolent in its livelihood). «Dhahaba damuhu baṭaran» means his blood was lost unavenged, treated lightly, for no retaliation was taken for it. «He is, in this matter, a learned veterinarian-expert», ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
ودعاني ما قال فيها عتيق ... وهو بالحسن عالم بيطار
(What ʿAtīq said of her drew me on, and he is, in beauty, a knowing connoisseur.)
«Al-baṭsh» is well known and has already been discussed. Of its figurative uses: "So-and-so strides in knowledge with an ample reach"; "the terrors of the world assailed them"; and of their sayings: "They traversed a land of distant roads and near perils, and were thrown into its assaults, and were not rescued from its thirsts". "The riding camels came shaking with their loads" (tabṭish bil-aḥmāl), that is, trembling with them. «Baṭṭa al-qarḥa bil-mibaṭṭ» means he lanced the sore with the lancet, which is the pressing out. "He has a «baṭṭa» of sesame oil." «Al-baṭṭ», singular «baṭṭa», for masculine and feminine, is a water bird with a short neck and short legs, different from the goose; its plural is «buṭūṭ» and «biṭāṭ». «Al-baṭṭa» is also a vessel like a flask. (Translator's note: the source then reads «أبطح، وهو باطل بين البطلان وبطّال بيّن البطالة بكسر الباء وقد بطل بفتح الطاء وبطل بيّن البطالة بفتح الباء وقد بطل بضم الطاء وقد بطل بضم الطاء أيضا», which is repetitive and appears garbled; it is rendered as follows.) «Abṭaḥ»; "he is «bāṭil», clearly futile (buṭlān)", and "a «baṭṭāl», clearly idle (baṭāla), with kasra on the bāʾ", and "he has become futile (baṭala) with fatḥa on the ṭāʾ", and "he became idle (baṭila) ... with fatḥa on the bāʾ, and has become futile (baṭula) with ḍamma on the ṭāʾ, and has become futile with ḍamma on the ṭāʾ also, he «yabṭul» with ḍamma, «baṭāla» and «buṭūla»", meaning he became brave; he is a «baṭal» (hero), plural «abṭāl», feminine «baṭala», plural «baṭalāt». «Al-baṭn» (belly) is well known. "The hen laid what was in her belly", and "the woman scattered her belly for the husband", when she bore many children; «baṭanahu wa-ẓahrahu» means he struck him on belly and back; «buṭina fulān», in the passive, when his belly is ailing, and he is «mabṭūn», «baṭīn», «mibṭān» and «mubṭin», that is, ailing in the belly or big-bellied. «Abṭana al-baʿīr» means he tightened its girth-belly (biṭāna); «bāṭantu ṣāḥibī» means I tied him with me; «baṭṭana thawbahu biṭāna ḥasana» means he lined his garment with a fine lining; «istabṭana amrahu» means he came to know its inner side; «tabaṭṭana al-kalaʾ» means he roamed in the pasture and went into its middle. Al-Khansāʾ said:
فجاء يبشّر أصحابه: تبطّنت يا قوم غيثا خصيبا
(He came giving his companions glad tidings: "O people, you have entered the middle of a fertile rain.")
«Tabaṭṭana al-jāriya» means he made her his confidante (biṭāna). Imruʾ al-Qays said:
كأني لم أركب جوادا للذّة ... ولم أتبطّن كاعبا ذات خلخال
(As though I had never ridden a noble steed for pleasure, nor taken as intimate a full-breasted girl wearing an anklet.)
One says "you are more intimate (abṭan) with this matter", meaning more knowing of its inner nature and longer in his acquaintance with it; "he is my confidant", "they are my confidants"; "so-and-so is wide of girth (ʿarīḍ al-biṭān)", that is, wealthy; and "a far goal (shaʾw baṭīn)", that is, distant. Zuhayr said:
فبصبص بين أداني الغضى ... وبين عنيزة شأوا بطينا
(It wagged its tail between the nearest ghaḍā trees and ʿUnayza, over a far-reaching distance.)

* I'rab:
(كَذَّبَتْ عادٌ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) A verb, agent and direct object; the clause is resumptive, brought to begin the fourth story. (إِذْ قالَ لَهُمْ أَخُوهُمْ هُودٌ أَلا تَتَّقُونَ) The adverb is attached to «كذبت»; «قال لهم أخوهم»: verb and agent; «هود» is a badal of «أخوهم»; «ألا» is a particle of offering; «تتقون» is an imperfect verb and agent, and the clause is the content of the saying. (إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ) The clause is a justification for his offering them the inclination towards piety. «إن» and its noun; «لكم» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial) or to «رسول»; «رسول» is the khabar of «إن» and «أمين» is an adjective of «رسول». (فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ) Its i'rab has been given many times. (وَما أَسْئَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْرٍ إِنْ أَجْرِيَ إِلَّا عَلى رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ) The i'rab of this was given word for word just above. (أَتَبْنُونَ بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ آيَةً تَعْبَثُونَ) The interrogative is for reproach and rebuke; «تبنون» is an imperfect verb and agent; «بكل ريع» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «تبنون»; «آية» is the direct object; and the clause «تعبثون» is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. (وَتَتَّخِذُونَ مَصانِعَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَخْلُدُونَ) «وتتخذون» is conjoined to «تبنون»; «تتخذون» is an imperfect verb and agent; «مصانع» is the direct object; «لعلكم تخلدون»: «لعل» and its noun, and the clause is its khabar; the clause of hope is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl, that is, hoping and expecting that you will abide forever in the world. (وَإِذا بَطَشْتُمْ بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; «إذا» is an adverb attached to the apodosis, which is the second «بطشتم»; the first clause «بطشتم» is in the position of the genitive because «إذا» is annexed to it; «جبارين» is a ḥāl, that is, not caring about results and consequences. He denounced this in them only because it was wrongdoing; as for striking with sword and whip in a rightful cause, it is permitted. (فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ) The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; «اتقوا الله»: imperative verb, agent and direct object; «أطيعون» is conjoined to «اتقوا».
(وَاتَّقُوا الَّذِي أَمَدَّكُمْ بِما تَعْلَمُونَ) «واتقوا»: imperative verb and agent; «الذي» is the direct object; the clause «أمدكم» is the ṣila; «بما» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «أمدكم», and the clause «تعلمون» is a ṣila.
(أَمَدَّكُمْ بِأَنْعامٍ وَبَنِينَ وَجَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ) The second clause «أمدكم» is a badal of the first clause «أمدكم», a badal of part from whole, because it is more specific than the first with regard to what each is attached to, so it is included in the first, since «ما تعلمون» includes livestock and other things. It was also said that it is explicative of the first clause, in which case it has no grammatical position. The discussion of a clause as a substitute for a clause will come in the section of Benefits. (إِنِّي أَخافُ عَلَيْكُمْ عَذابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ) «إن» and its noun, and the clause «أخاف» is its khabar; «عليكم» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «أخاف»; «عذاب» is the direct object; «يوم» is muḍāf ilayhi; «عظيم» is an adjective. (قالُوا سَواءٌ عَلَيْنا أَوَعَظْتَ أَمْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مِنَ الْواعِظِينَ) «سواء» is an advanced khabar; «علينا» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «سواء»; the hamza is interrogative; «وعظت» is a past verb and agent; «أم لم تكن من الواعظين» is the counterpart of His saying «أوعظت»; the hamza of equalization and what is within its scope are in the interpretation of a maṣdar, a delayed mubtadaʾ, that is, "your admonishing is equal to us". He brought the counterpart in this way rather than saying «أم لم تعظ» for the sake of the rhymes. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "There is a difference between them, because the meaning is: it is equal to us whether you performed this act, which is admonition, or were not at all one of its people and practitioners; this is stronger in expressing how little they regard his admonition than your saying «أم لم تعظ»." (إِنْ هذا إِلَّا خُلُقُ الْأَوَّلِينَ) «إن» is negative; «هذا» is mubtadaʾ; «إلا» is a particle of restriction; «خلق» is the khabar of «هذا»; «الأولين» is muḍāf ilayhi. The meaning: this religion we are upon is nothing but the habit of the ancients and their custom; they practised it and we follow them. (وَما نَحْنُ بِمُعَذَّبِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; «ما» is the negative Ḥijāzī «mā»; «نحن» is its noun; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition; «معذبين» is genitive in form by the bāʾ and accusative in position as the khabar of «ما».
(فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَهْلَكْناهُمْ إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً وَما كانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; «كذبوه»: past verb, agent and direct object; «فأهلكناهم» is conjoined to «فكذبوه»; «إن» is a particle resembling the verb; «في ذلك» is the khabar of «إن»; the shifted lām; «آية» is the noun of «إن»; the wāw is a conjunction; «ما» is negative; «كان» is a defective past verb; «أكثرهم» is its noun and «مؤمنين» its khabar. (وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ) Its i'rab has been repeated many times.

* Benefits:
A clause may be a substitute for a clause, on condition that the second clause is fuller than the first in conveying what is intended; therefore the congruent badal (badal muṭābiq) does not occur among clauses; what occurs is the badal of part from whole, as earlier in the verse, or the badal al-ishtimāl (inclusive substitute), as in his saying:
أقول له ارحل لا تقيمنّ عندنا ... وإلّا فكن في السرّ والجهر مسلما
(I say to him: depart, do not stay with us; otherwise be, in secret and in public, a Muslim.)
«فلا تقيمنّ عندنا» is a badal al-ishtimāl of «ارحل», because of the necessary connection between them. It is not emphasis of it, because their wordings differ; nor a badal of part from whole, because it is not included in the first; nor a congruent badal, because it is not regarded as a replacement. The grammarians did not require a pronoun in the badal of part and the badal al-ishtimāl in verbs and clauses, since a pronoun cannot return to them. A clause may also be a substitute for a single word as a congruent badal, as in al-Farazdaq's saying:
إلى الله أشكو بالمدينة حاجة ... وبالشام أخرى كيف يلتقيان
(To Allah I complain of a need in Medina and another in Syria: how can the two meet?)
He made the clause «كيف يلتقيان» a badal of «حاجة» and «أخرى», which are single words. This is sound because the clause reverts to being interpreted as a single word, that is, "To Allah I complain of these two needs, the impossibility of their meeting"; so «taʿadhdhur» (impossibility) is a maṣdar annexed to its agent, and it is a badal of «hātayn». Some grammarians did not concede this, since the clause «كيف يلتقيان» may be resumptive, by which he draws attention to the reason for the complaint, which is the improbability of these two needs coming together.
Some said: and is the reverse permissible, I mean substituting a single word for a clause, or not? Abū Ḥayyān stated in al-Baḥr that a single word may be a badal of a clause, as in the saying of the Exalted «ولم يجعل له عوجا قيما»: for him «قيما» is a badal of the clause «لم يجعل له عوجا», because it is in the sense of a single word, that is, "He made it straight". Ibn Hishām said in Mughnī al-Labīb: "The clause «كيف خلقت» is a badal al-ishtimāl of «الإبل», and the meaning is 'to the camels, the manner of their creation'; and like it «ألم تر إلى ربك كيف مد الظل»; and every clause in which there is «kayfa» is in the place of a single noun."
An important benefit:
When a noun is substituted for an interrogative noun or a conditional noun, it is obligatory to mention the interrogative hamza or the conditional «in» with the badal, so that it agrees with what is substituted for in meaning, as in: «كم مالك؟ أعشرون أم ثلاثون»: «كم» is an interrogative noun in the position of the nominative as an advanced khabar, «مالك» is a delayed mubtadaʾ, and «عشرون» is a badal of «كم»; the grammarians call it badal tafṣīl (detailing substitute), and it is limited to the congruent kind. And «من جاءك أعلي أم خالد؟»: «من» is an interrogative noun in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ, the clause «جاءك» is its khabar, and «علي» is a badal tafṣīl of the interrogative «من». And like «من يجتهد إن علي أو خالد فأكرمه»: «من» is a jussive-governing conditional noun in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ and the clause after it is its khabar; «إن» is a conditional particle with no operation here, because it was brought to clarify the meaning and not to operate; «علي» is a badal of the latent pronoun in «يجتهد»; «خالد» is conjoined to «علي»; and the clause «فأكرمه» is in the position of the jussive as the apodosis. And like «حيثما تنتظرني في المدرسة وإن في الدار أوافك»: «حيثما» is a jussive-governing conditional noun in the position of the accusative as an adverbial object, attached to «تنتظرني»; «في المدرسة» is a preposition and its genitive noun in the position of the accusative as a badal of the position of «حيثما».

dervis-irab:52-68.t:
* Vocabulary:
(لَشِرْذِمَةٌ): The shirdhima is a small group of people; its plural is sharādhim and sharādhīm. Thiyāb sharādhim means torn garments, and sharradha al-jamʿ (with doubling) means he scattered the gathering.
(حاذِرُونَ): Alert (mutayaqqiẓūn). It is an intensive form of the active participle, and it was also read ḥādhirūn. Abū ʿUbayda said: The two are of one meaning; one says rajul ḥadhir and ḥādhir with one meaning. It is also said that there is a difference between them: the ḥadhir is the alert one and the ḥādhir the fearful one; and it is said that the ḥadhir is one created and disposed to caution, and the ḥādhir is one in whom that has befallen. In al-Miṣbāḥ:
"Ḥadhira ḥadharan (of the pattern taʿiba), and iḥtadhara and iḥtaraza all have one meaning: he prepared and made ready, so he is ḥādhir and ḥadhir, and the noun from it is al-ḥadhar like ḥamal. Ḥadhira al-shayʾ means he feared it, so the thing is maḥdhūr, that is, feared; and ḥadhartuhu al-shayʾ, so he is wary of it." In another reading, ḥādirūn with the unpointed dāl; the ḥādir is the fat, strong one. He said:
أحب الصبي السوء من أجل أمه ... وأبغضه من بغضها وهو حادر
(Gloss: I love the bad boy for the sake of his mother, and I hate him out of hatred of her, though he is stout.)
That is, the basis of loving a child is love for his mother, not the goodness of his qualities. The pronoun in أبغضه refers to the boy without his description, but this is the disposition of one immersed in the love of women.
(مُشْرِقِينَ): Entering the time of sunrise (shurūq), from sharaqat al-shams shurūqan when it rose.
(فِرْقٍ): With a kasra on the fāʾ, that is, a piece.
(الطود): The mountain, or its great mass, as in al-Qāmūs; the plural is aṭwād, and ṭāda yaṭūdu means he was firm.
(وَأَزْلَفْنا): We brought near.

* I'rab:
(وَأَوْحَيْنا إِلى مُوسى أَنْ أَسْرِ بِعِبادِي إِنَّكُمْ مُتَّبَعُونَ) The wāw is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive, to begin the command directed to Moses to travel by night with his people toward the sea, which was thirty years after the events mentioned above. أوحينا is a verb and agent; إلى موسى is a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to أوحينا; أن is explicative, because in revelation there is the meaning of saying without its letters; أسر is an imperative from asrā, that is, he travelled by night. In another reading, with a kasra on the nūn and the hamza of أسر as a connecting hamza, from sarā, a dialect form of asrā. بعبادي is attached to أسر or is a ḥāl, that is, "accompanied by my servants"; the clause إنكم متبعون is a justification of the command to travel by night. (فَأَرْسَلَ فِرْعَوْنُ فِي الْمَدائِنِ حاشِرِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction, even though in time there was a gap, because, as is reported, they were occupied with burying their dead from the plague that swept Egypt; أرسل فرعون is a verb and agent; في المدائن is a ḥāl; and حاشرين is the direct object. (إِنَّ هؤُلاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ) The clause is the content of an omitted saying, accusative as a ḥāl, that is, "saying"; إن with its noun, the shifted lām, and شرذمة its khabar; قليلون is an adjective, because they were a minority, small [Translator's note: the source prints «فسئيلة؟؟؟», an illegible word followed by three question marks] in relation to Pharaoh's people. The secret of the sound masculine plural for a small group will come in the chapter on rhetoric. (وَإِنَّهُمْ لَنا لَغائِظُونَ) The wāw is a conjunction or ḥāl; إن with its noun; لنا is attached to غائظون; the shifted lām; and غائظون is the khabar of إن, that is, "doers of what angers us". (وَإِنَّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ) The wāw is a conjunction or ḥāl; إن with its noun; the shifted lām; جميع is a first khabar and حذرون [Translator's note: the source prints «حذرون» rather than «حاذرون»] a second khabar, that is, "we are a people whose habit is alertness, caution and the use of resolve in affairs". Pharaoh wanted to cover the breach that had struck his awe, so he described himself and his clan with the most emphatic descriptions indicating firmness of rank and strength of spirit. (فَأَخْرَجْناهُمْ مِنْ جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ) The fāʾ is resumptive; أخرجناهم is a verb, agent and direct object; من جنات وعيون is attached to أخرجناهم. He meant the orchards that lay on both banks of the Nile and the small rivers branching from the Nile and distributed among the houses. A lengthy description of Egypt will come in the section of benefits. (وَكُنُوزٍ وَمَقامٍ كَرِيمٍ) Conjoined to جنات وعيون. By "treasures" he meant the wealth beneath the earth, and singled it out because what was above it had its landmarks effaced, or because they had not spent it on what ought to be spent on goodness.
(كَذلِكَ وَأَوْرَثْناها بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ) كذلك is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, that is, "We brought them out in the like of that bringing-out". It is permissible to parse the kāf as an adjective of مقام كريم, that is, "a station like that station which they had"; and it is permissible to parse the kāf as nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "the matter is thus". وأورثناها: the wāw is a conjunction or parenthetical, and the latter is perhaps preferable; أورثناها is a verb, agent and first direct object, and بني إسرائيل a second direct object, that is, after the drowning of Pharaoh and his people. (فَأَتْبَعُوهُمْ مُشْرِقِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; أتبعوهم is a past verb, agent and second direct object [Translator's note: the source says «مفعول به ثان», "second direct object", though only the pronoun object is given], that is, they caught up with them; and مشرقين is a ḥāl. (فَلَمَّا تَراءَا الْجَمْعانِ قالَ أَصْحابُ مُوسى إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; لما is temporal, adverbial, or a connective; تراءى الجمعان is a past verb and agent, that is, they faced each other and each saw the other; the clause قال has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of لما; أصحاب is the agent of قال; and the clause إنا لمدركون is the content of the saying. (قالَ كَلَّا إِنَّ مَعِي رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ) قال موسى; كلا is a particle of rebuke and reproach. Moses wished to cast blame upon them for the weakness of their nerves and the slackness of their resolve, that is, "they will never overtake us". Then إن معي is a justification for this rebuke; إن is a particle resembling the verb; the adverbial is attached to an omitted element which is a fronted khabar, and ربي is its postponed noun; the clause سيهدين is resumptive. He erred who parsed it as a ḥāl, and the detail will come in the section of benefits. (فَأَوْحَيْنا إِلى مُوسى أَنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ الْبَحْرَ فَانْفَلَقَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; أوحينا is a verb and agent; إلى موسى is attached to أوحينا; أن is explicative; اضرب بعصاك البحر is an imperative, a latent agent and a direct object; بعصاك is attached to اضرب; and in فانفلق the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ, which has often gone before, that is, "he struck, and so it split". (فَكانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; كان with its noun; the kāf is a noun in the sense of "like", its khabar, or it is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted khabar; and العظيم is an adjective of الطود. (وَأَزْلَفْنا ثَمَّ الْآخَرِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; أزلفنا is a verb and agent; ثم is an adverbial in the sense of "there"; and الآخرين is the direct object. By them he meant Pharaoh's people, that is, "We brought them near to Moses' people".
(وَأَنْجَيْنا مُوسى وَمَنْ مَعَهُ أَجْمَعِينَ) وأنجينا is conjoined to what precedes; it is a verb and agent; موسى is the direct object; من is conjoined to موسى; معه is an adverbial of place attached to an omitted element which is the ṣila of من; and أجمعين is an emphasis of من. (ثُمَّ أَغْرَقْنَا الْآخَرِينَ) Conjoined to what precedes. (إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً وَما كانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) A justification of what went before, that is, "We made that and decreed it only that it should be a sign and an admonition for people, but most of them did not take heed of it". في ذلك is the fronted khabar of إن; the shifted lām; the wāw is a conjunction; ما is negative; كان with its noun; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition [Translator's note: the source says «والباء حرف جر زائد» although no bāʾ appears in this verse as printed; the reference is to the form in the surah's refrain, which has not occurred in the verse text here; translated as written] and مؤمنين is genitive in form, accusative in position, as the khabar of كان. The redundancy of the bāʾ in the khabar of كان will come in the section of benefits. (وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ) Conjoined to what precedes; إن with its noun; the shifted lām; هو is a separating pronoun or a mubtadaʾ; and العزيز الرحيم are two khabars of إن, or of هو, the clause being the khabar of إن.

* Rhetoric:
In the words of the Exalted «إن هؤلاء لشرذمة قليلون»: the shirdhima is the small group or party, as we mentioned in the section on vocabulary, and it would have been possible to be content with it as an expression of fewness; but he described it with "the fewest of the few" to increase their contempt and belittle their standing; then he pluralised their description so that it be known that every class of them is few; and he chose the sound masculine plural, which is the plural of paucity. These are four aspects that support one another in making them few. There is also a fifth aspect, which is that pluralising the adjective while the described is singular may be an exaggeration in the adherence of that description to the described and its extremity in it in relation to other described things. Reflect on this, for it is among the finest subtleties.

* Benefits:
1- Conditions for a ḥāl to be a clause:
A ḥāl is a clause on three conditions:
1- The clause must be declarative (khabariyya), that is, one that admits truth and falsehood. This condition is agreed upon, because the ḥāl is like the adjective, and the adjective cannot be a performative (inshāʾī) clause. As for what occurs in the hadith: «Do not sell gold for gold except hāʾ wa-hāʾ ["take and give"]», it is based on an implied saying, that is, "except saying hāʾ and hāʾ", from the side of the seller and the buyer.
In al-Murādī's commentary on al-Tashīl, the declarative includes the conditional, and it is permissible for it to occur as a ḥāl; but the statement of al-Mughnī contradicts it. The verified view is that regarding the conditional clause, if the speech is the apodosis and the condition is a restriction upon it, then if the apodosis is a declarative, the conditional clause is declarative, and if performative, performative; and if the speech is the whole of the condition and apodosis, it is not declarative, because the particle has taken it out of that.
Moreover, he erred who said, regarding the verse of one of the later poets:
أطلب ولا تضجر من مطلب ... فآفة الطالب أن يضجرا
أما ترى الحبل بتكراره ... في الصخرة الصمّاء قد أثرا
(Gloss: Seek, and do not grow weary of seeking, for the bane of the seeker is to grow weary. Do you not see the rope, by its repetition, has left its mark in the solid rock?)
that لا is prohibitive and that the wāw is the ḥāl-wāw. Ibn Hishām says in al-Mughnī: This is an error, and the correct view regarding the wāw is that it is a conjunction, either [conjoining] a maṣdar made up from أن and the verb, onto a maṣdar imagined from the preceding command, that is, "let there be from you seeking and non-wearying", or a clause onto a clause. On the first, the fatḥa of تضجر is an inflectional sign and لا is negative; on the second, the fatḥa is indeclinable by reason of composition, the original being ولا تضجرن with the light nūn of emphasis, which was dropped out of necessity, and لا is prohibitive, the conjunction being like «واعبدوا الله ولا تشركوا به شيئا». Then Ibn Hishām resumed his statement in al-Mughnī in the eighth type of the sixth aspect and said: "The sounder view is that the fatḥa, meaning the fatḥa of تضجر, is inflectional, like that in لا تأكل السمك وتشرب اللبن, not indeclinable because of an omitted nūn of emphasis."
2- The clause must not be introduced by an indication of futurity, because the purpose of the ḥāl is to specify the occurrence of the content of its governor with the time of occurrence of the content of the ḥāl, and that contradicts futurity. He erred who parsed «سيهدين» in the words of the Exalted «إني ذاهب إلى ربي سيهدين» as a ḥāl. The error is evident from the technical side; and as for the side of meaning, he made the meaning of the verse "I shall go guided", thus diverting the extension of time to the going, whereas in the verse it belongs to the guidance. It was answered that "guided" occurs after the going, in which there is an extension, so it must also have an extension, like the restricted. As for their saying «لأضربنه إن ذهب وإن مكث», a conditional clause was permitted there as a ḥāl although introduced by an indication of futurity, namely إن, because the meaning is "I shall strike him in every case", since it is not valid to stipulate the existence and the non-existence of a thing for one and the same thing.
3- It must be linked either by the wāw and the pronoun together, to strengthen the link, as in «ألم تر إلى الذين خرجوا من ديارهم وهم ألوف حذر الموت»: the clause هم ألوف is a ḥāl from the wāw in خرجوا, linked by the wāw and the pronoun, which is هم; or by the pronoun alone without the wāw, as in «اهبطوا بعضكم لبعض عدو»: بعضكم is a mubtadaʾ and عدو its khabar, and لبعض is attached to عدو or is a ḥāl from it, and the clause is a ḥāl from the wāw in اهبطوا, that is, "enemies to each other, each misleading the other", and it is linked by the pronoun alone, which is the kāf and mīm; or linked by the wāw alone without the pronoun, as in «لئن أكله الذئب ونحن عصبة»: the clause ونحن عصبة is a ḥāl from الذئب, linked by the wāw only, and نحن has no part in the linking since it does not refer back to the owner of the ḥāl.
2- The description of Egypt to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ:
When ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ became settled in the governorship of Egypt, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to him: "Describe Egypt to me." He wrote back to him: "The letter of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah prolong his life, has come, asking me about Egypt. Know, Commander of the Faithful, that Egypt is a dusty village and a green tree, its length a month and its breadth ten [days]. A dusty mountain and a dune of sand flank it, and in its midst strides a Nile blessed in its mornings, auspicious in its evenings, in which increase and decrease run like the course of the sun and the moon. It has a season in which it yields its milk and its flies multiply; the springs and wells of the earth feed it, until, when its flood has swollen and its waves have grown mighty, it overflows both its banks, and no escape from one village to another is possible except in small boats, light craft and skiffs which in appearance are like the leaves of the evening. Then, when it has completed its rise, it turns back on its heels as it first appeared in its course, and withdraws within its bounds. At that time a despised community and a guarded people go out, who plough the land and sow grain in it, hoping thereby for growth from the Lord; what they strive for by their toil is for others, who obtain it from them without their effort. When the crop surrounds and shines, the dew waters it and the soil beneath nourishes it. So while Egypt, Commander of the Faithful, is a white pearl, behold, it is black ambergris; then behold, it is a green emerald; then behold, it is a variegated brocade. Blessed be Allah, the Creator of what He wills." — to the end of that delightful letter.
In al-Maqrīzī's Khiṭaṭ there is what clears up the obscurities of this letter:
"Some of them described Egypt and said: Three months it is a white pearl, three months a black musk, three months a green emerald, and three months a red ingot of gold. As for the white pearl, in the months of Abīb, Masrā and Tūt the water mounts over it, and you see the world white, with its estates on rises and hillocks like stars encircled by water from every side, so there is no way to any of its villages except by skiffs. As for the black musk, in the months of Bāba, Hātūr and Kīhak the water uncovers from the land, which turns into black earth, and in these months the sowing takes place. As for the green emerald, in the months of Ṭūba, Amshīr and Baramhāt the plants of the land and its spring multiply, and it becomes green as though it were an emerald. As for the red ingot, in the months of Baramūda, Bashans and Baʾūna the herbage reddens and the crop reaches harvest, and it is like an ingot of gold in appearance and benefit."
3- The redundancy of the bāʾ in the khabar of كان:
Laysa and kāna are distinguished by the permissibility of a redundant bāʾ in their khabars. Its redundancy is frequent in the khabar of laysa and of the Ḥijāzī mā; as for kāna, it is not made redundant except when preceded by negation or prohibition, as in the verse and as in the words of al-Shanfarā:
وإن مدّت الأيدي إلى الزاد لم أكن ... بأعجلهم إذا أجشع القوم أعجل
(Gloss: If hands are stretched toward the provisions, I am not the hastiest of them, when the people are most greedy, the hastiest.)

dervis-irab:141-159.t:
* Vocabulary:
(نَخْلٍ): «Al-nakhl» and «al-nakhīl» is the well-known date-bearing tree, with a straight, tall trunk with knots; the singular is «nakhla» and «nakhīla». In al-Miṣbāḥ, in summary: «al-nakhl» is a collective noun, the singular being «nakhla», and every collective noun of this sort is used as feminine and masculine; as for «al-nakhīl», with yāʾ, it is feminine by agreement.
(طَلْعُها هَضِيمٌ): What comes out of it like the blade of a sword, in whose interior are the stalks of the date cluster; it is likened to a sword blade in form and shape. In al-Mukhtār: "The spathe (ṭalʿ) is called «haḍīm» as long as it has not come out, because parts of it are folded into others", from their saying «kashḥ haḍīm» (a slender flank). In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj: "«Al-ṭalʿ» is a measure; you say 'the army is a ṭalʿ of a thousand'; and from the palm, something that comes out like two sandals joined together, with the fruit set in rows between them and the tip pointed; or what appears of its fruit at the beginning of its emergence." «Al-haḍīm» is the ripe, soft, tender, delicate.
(فارِهِينَ): It was also read «farihīn»: exultant, skilled in work, from «al-farah», which is intense joy. He said in al-Kashshāf: "«Al-farāha» is cleverness and vigour; from it 'a spirited horse' (khayl farha)."
(شِرْبٌ): With kasra on the shīn, meaning a share.
(فَعَقَرُوها): That is, one of them struck her with the sword on her legs. His name was Qudār. We shall relate the story that was woven around this story, to be an incentive for pens to compose an artistic story from it.

* I'rab:
(كَذَّبَتْ ثَمُودُ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) A resumptive clause, brought to begin the fifth story; it is a verb, agent and direct object. «Thamūd» is the name of Ṣāliḥ's tribe, named after their father, Thamūd, the grandfather of Ṣāliḥ. As to the expression of Ṣāliḥ in the plural, what was said earlier applies.
(إِذْ قالَ لَهُمْ أَخُوهُمْ صالِحٌ أَلا تَتَّقُونَ) The adverb is attached to «كذبت»; the i'rab of the clause has been given. (إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ) Its i'rab has also been given.
(فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ) Its i'rab has also been given. (وَما أَسْئَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْرٍ إِنْ أَجْرِيَ إِلَّا عَلى رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ) Its i'rab has also been given. (أَتُتْرَكُونَ فِي ما هاهُنا آمِنِينَ) The hamza is for the interrogative of denial and rebuke; «تتركون» is a passive imperfect verb; «فيما» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «تتركون»; «ها» is a particle of attention; «هنا» is a demonstrative in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place, attached to an omitted ṣila of the relative; «آمنين» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the wāw in «تتركون», that is, in that bliss which is settled in this place; then He explained it by His saying: (فِي جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ وَزُرُوعٍ وَنَخْلٍ طَلْعُها هَضِيمٌ) «في جنات» is a badal of His saying «فيما هاهنا», with the preposition repeated; what follows is conjoined to «جنات»; «طلعها» is mubtadaʾ and «هضيم» is khabar, and the clause is an adjective of «نخل».
(وَتَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبالِ بُيُوتاً فارِهِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; «تنحتون» is conjoined to «تتركون», so it is within the scope of the interrogative of denial and rebuke, and the position of the rebuking interrogative clause is accusative as a ḥāl; «من الجبال» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «تنحتون»; «بيوتا» is the direct object; «فارهين» is a ḥāl. A similar clause has already passed, in which was the carving (naḥt), which is cutting and shaping. (فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ) Its i'rab has been given.
(وَلا تُطِيعُوا أَمْرَ الْمُسْرِفِينَ) The wāw is for ḥāl, and «لا» is prohibitive; «تطيعوا» is an imperfect verb, jussive by the prohibitive «لا», and the wāw is the agent; «أمر المسرفين» is the object. The meaning of obeying a command will come in the section of Rhetoric. (الَّذِينَ يُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلا يُصْلِحُونَ) «الذين» is an adjective of «المسرفين»; the clause «يفسدون» is the ṣila; «في الأرض» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «يفسدون»; «ولا يصلحون» is conjoined to His saying «يفسدون». The secret of the conjunction will come in the section of Rhetoric. (قالُوا: إِنَّما أَنْتَ مِنَ الْمُسَحَّرِينَ) «إنما» is the restraining particle with the restrained; «أنت» is mubtadaʾ and «من المسحرين» is the khabar, that is, those who were bewitched so much that the sorcery overcame their minds; the clause is the content of the saying. It was also said that «al-musaḥḥar» is the one who is sustained by food and drink, so «al-musaḥḥar» is the one who has a «saḥr», which is the lung; so it is as though they said, "You are only a human like us, who eats and drinks."
(ما أَنْتَ إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُنا فَأْتِ بِآيَةٍ إِنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ) «ما» is negative; «أنت» is mubtadaʾ; «إلا» is a particle of restriction; «بشر» is the khabar and «مثلنا» an adjective. In «فأت» the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ, that is, "if you are truthful as you claim, then bring"; «بآية» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to His saying «فأت»; «إن» is conditional; «كنت»: «kāna» and its noun, in the position of the jussive as the protasis; «من الصادقين» is the khabar of «كنت»; the apodosis of «إن» is omitted, indicated by what precedes, that is, "then bring a sign".
(قالَ هذِهِ ناقَةٌ لَها شِرْبٌ وَلَكُمْ شِرْبُ يَوْمٍ مَعْلُومٍ) «هذه» is mubtadaʾ and «ناقة» is khabar, and the clause is the content of the saying; «لها» is an advanced khabar and «شرب» a delayed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is an adjective of «ناقة»; «لكم» is an advanced khabar and «شرب يوم» a delayed mubtadaʾ; «معلوم» is an adjective of «يوم».
(وَلا تَمَسُّوها بِسُوءٍ فَيَأْخُذَكُمْ عَذابُ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ) The wāw is a conjunction; «لا» is prohibitive; «تمسوها» is an imperfect verb, jussive by «لا», the wāw is the agent and the hāʾ the direct object; «بسوء» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «تمسوها»; in «فيأخذكم» the fāʾ is the fāʾ of causation and «يأخذكم» is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied «أن» after the fāʾ; the kāf is the direct object; «عذاب» is the agent, «يوم» is muḍāf ilayhi and «عظيم» is an adjective of «يوم». (فَعَقَرُوها فَأَصْبَحُوا نادِمِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; «عقروها»: verb, agent and direct object; in «فأصبحوا» the fāʾ is a conjunction, and «أصبحوا نادمين»: «aṣbaḥa» is a defective past verb, the wāw is its noun and «نادمين» its khabar. You may also make «أصبحوا» a complete verb, the wāw the agent and «نادمين» a ḥāl; in the story of Ṣāliḥ there will come what favours its being complete. (فَأَخَذَهُمُ الْعَذابُ إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً وَما كانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; «أخذهم» is a past verb with an advanced direct object, and «العذاب» is a delayed agent; the clause «إن في ذلك لآية» is a justification for the seizing; the wāw is a ḥāl wāw or a conjunction; «ما» is negative; «كان» with its noun and khabar. (وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ) Its i'rab has been given many times.

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying «ولا تطيعوا أمر المسرفين» there is a mental figurative expression (majāz ʿaqlī), because a command is not obeyed; the one obeyed is the one who gives it, that is, "do not obey the transgressors in their command".
2- Al-irdāf (the follow-on):
It would have sufficed to say «الذين يفسدون في الأرض», but since His saying «يفسدون» does not negate their being at times righteous, He followed it with His saying «ولا يصلحون» to show the perfection of their corruption and of their transgression in it.

* Benefits:
The story of Ṣāliḥ:
In al-Qurṭubī: "Allah revealed to Ṣāliḥ that his people would hamstring his she-camel, so he told them that. They said, 'We would never do it.' Ṣāliḥ said to them, 'In this month of yours a boy will be born who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands.' They said, 'No male will be born this month but we will kill him.' Nine of them had sons born in that month and they slaughtered their sons; then to the tenth one, who refused to slaughter his son, a son was born, and none had been born to him before. The tenth man's son was blue-eyed and ruddy and grew up quickly. Whenever he passed the nine and they saw him, they said, 'If our sons were alive they would be like this.' The nine were angry with Ṣāliḥ because he had been the cause of their killing their sons, so they banded together and swore by Allah, 'We will attack him and his family by night.' They said, 'We will go out on a journey so that people see our journey, and we will be in a cave; when night comes and Ṣāliḥ goes out to his mosque, we will come to him and kill him. Then we will say: we did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are truthful. They will believe us and know that we had gone out on a journey.' Ṣāliḥ did not sleep with them in the village but slept in the mosque, and when morning came he went to them and admonished them. When they entered the cave and wished to come out, the cave fell upon them and killed them. People who had learned of this saw it and cried out in the village, 'O servants of Allah! Was Ṣāliḥ not satisfied to order them to kill their children until he killed them?' So the people of the village agreed on hamstringing the she-camel."
The account of the hamstringing of the she-camel:
It is related that Miṣdaʿ drove the she-camel into a narrow place in a mountain path and shot her with an arrow, which hit her leg, and she fell; then Qudār struck her. It was also said that he said, "I will not hamstring her until all of you agree."
